before: Cyberattack detection and alarm clearance impose different demands on a robotic digital twin. A predictor can follow unauthorized motion, while an inaccurate reference can prevent clearance after recovery. This study separates physical return from reference proximity and examines three sources of error: model mismatch, measurement noise and continuing motion. In 216 synthetic episodes, thirteen monitoring rules receive common observations and approved-command context. Adding an empirical uncertainty allowance reduces benign alarm observations from 621 to 309 relative to nominal fixed return, but permits timely clearance in only 36 of 108 detected events with physical return. Removing the allowance at the same entry threshold yields 140 benign alarm observations and 108 timely clearances, with no observed premature clearing. A normal-only search over 63 reference models reduces the allowance by 51.27\% and 38.56\% on the harder plants without satisfying the overall feasibility requirement. A conditional Gaussian calculation explains how a noisy calibration maximum can exhaust the recovery tolerance even with a perfect reference. A subsequent covariance-aware window control meets a predeclared normal-feasibility criterion on 20 of 36 synthetic residual traces; correlation and changing motion limit the benefit of averaging. A separate common-input IMU study records improved CASPER-style training adequacy, with an ordinary autoregressive control retaining the lowest normal prediction error. These results support an evaluation discipline for recovery monitoring: distinguish prediction from physical return, account for uncertainty explicitly, and establish normal-operation feasibility before interpreting reduced alarm burden as a security improvement.
after: A robotic digital twin may detect a motion anomaly yet give poor evidence about when the alarm should clear. Its predictor may follow unauthorized motion, or its reference may remain inaccurate after the robot recovers. We examine this problem by separating physical return from agreement with a reference model. Thirteen monitoring rules are compared on 216 synthetic episodes using the same observations and approved commands. An empirical uncertainty allowance reduces benign alarm observations from 621 to 309 relative to nominal fixed return, but allows timely clearance in only 36 of 108 detected events with physical return. Removing the allowance while keeping the entry threshold gives 140 benign alarm observations and 108 timely clearances, with no observed premature clearing. A search over 63 reference models fitted to normal data reduces the allowance by 51.27\% and 38.56\% on the harder plants, yet the overall feasibility requirement still fails. A Gaussian calculation explains why calibration noise can consume the recovery tolerance even with a perfect reference. A covariance-aware window control then meets the declared normal-feasibility criterion on 20 of 36 synthetic residual traces; temporal correlation and changing motion limit the gains from averaging. In a separate common-input inertial measurement unit (IMU) study, longer CASPER-style training lowers prediction error, but an ordinary autoregressive control remains strongest. The findings show why reduced alarm burden must be assessed alongside physical recovery, and why a clearance rule should first be checked on normal motion.

before: A robot can continue to move away from its intended trajectory after a corrupted command has been removed. An alarm that clears at command restoration can therefore disappear before the physical effect ends. The reverse problem also occurs: an accurate account of the robot's recovery may remain inconsistent with an inaccurate nominal model, leaving an alarm active after normal motion resumes. Both errors matter when a digital twin supplies evidence for cyberattack monitoring.
after: Removing a corrupted command does not immediately undo its effect on a robot. The arm may still be displaced or moving away from its intended trajectory when the controller resumes approved commands. Clearing an alarm at that instant can hide the remaining deviation. An inaccurate nominal model creates the opposite problem: the robot recovers, but the alarm stays active because the measurements still disagree with the model. A twin used for cyberattack monitoring must therefore support decisions about both the onset and the end of abnormal motion.

before: Recent robotic anomaly detectors use motion measurements to identify departures from expected behavior~\cite{casper,edge}. Hybrid twins combine models of robot mechanics, drives and control with learned components~\cite{hybrid}. These approaches motivate a closer examination of the relationship between prediction quality and alarm recovery. A small one-step prediction error need not indicate a return to authorized motion, because the predictor may already be following the deviation. Conversely, a large free-reference error can reflect ordinary model mismatch rather than a continuing attack.
after: Recent robotic anomaly detectors identify departures from expected behavior in motion measurements~\cite{casper,edge}, while hybrid twins combine learned components with models of robot mechanics, drives and control~\cite{hybrid}. Prediction error is useful in both settings, but its meaning depends on how the reference evolves. A predictor corrected by recent measurements may follow an unauthorized deviation and produce a small error. A reference that runs without correction may produce a large error simply because its model is inaccurate. Neither observation, by itself, tells us whether the robot has returned to authorized motion.

before: We study a specific question: \emph{under model mismatch, when does discrepancy from a command-driven reference provide usable evidence for clearing a robotic attack alarm?} The monitor receives noisy joint positions and velocities together with a protected record of approved commands. An attacker can corrupt the downstream command path. This information model permits a reference to predict authorized motion while preserving a distinction between approved and executed commands.
after: The question addressed here is: \emph{under model mismatch, when does discrepancy from a command-driven reference provide usable evidence for clearing a robotic attack alarm?} We assume access to noisy joint positions and velocities and a protected record of approved commands. The attacker can alter commands downstream of that record. This gives the monitor a way to predict authorized motion even when the plant executes a different command.

before: The investigation has three connected stages. A prospectively specified attack evaluation compares thirteen detection and clearance rules under common observations. A subsequent normal-only study tests whether better clean-data identification restores clearance feasibility. A Gaussian analysis and a separately specified residual experiment then examine noise allocation, temporal correlation and the cost of bounding current rather than average motion. Later stages diagnose the initial failure without revising its attack results. A separate external-IMU prediction study, reported in Appendix~\ref{app:imu}, checks the training adequacy of recent architectural comparators without giving them access to the simulated command context.
after: We first compare thirteen detection and clearance rules under a fixed attack protocol. When the uncertainty-based rule fails to clear reliably, we examine whether better references fitted to clean data resolve the problem. A Gaussian calculation and a separate residual experiment isolate the effects of measurement noise, temporal correlation and motion during the averaging window. These later analyses explain the initial failure; the original attack results remain unchanged. Appendix~\ref{app:imu} reports a separate external inertial measurement unit (IMU) prediction study that checks training adequacy under common inputs, without giving those predictors the simulation's command information.

before: The contribution is an experimentally supported account of a failure mode in uncertainty-based alarm clearance. It combines a physical-return target, matched component comparisons, normal-reference development and explicit noise calculations. The window experiment further identifies when averaging restores a usable return margin and when its motion penalty prevents that benefit. The bounds use established interval and probability arguments. AFTER names this investigation; it does not denote a newly validated detector or a claimed improvement over complete recent systems.
after: The paper contributes an experimentally supported explanation of a failure in uncertainty-based alarm clearance. Matched comparisons identify the component responsible, while reference fitting and noise calculations explain why the difficulty persists. The window experiment shows when averaging recovers enough margin to recognize normal motion and when variation within the window prevents it. The mathematical bounds use established interval and probability arguments. AFTER is the name of this investigation; it does not denote a newly validated detector or establish an improvement over complete recent systems.

before: CASPER detects anomalous industrial-arm motion using external inertial sensing and contextual information~\cite{casper}. Its edge-computing successor develops real-time robotic anomaly detection~\cite{edge}. Their sensing modality differs from the joint-state and approved-command simulation here. Appendix~\ref{app:imu} evaluates independently written architectural implementations on the same nominal IMU observations, with causal preprocessing and ordinary controls. This separate study supports a normal prediction comparison; it does not reproduce either paper's attack benchmark or justify ranking IMU-only predictors against command-aware recovery monitors.
after: CASPER uses external inertial sensing and contextual information to detect anomalous industrial-arm motion~\cite{casper}. Its successor develops real-time detection with edge computing~\cite{edge}. Those inputs differ from the joint states and approved commands available in our simulation. To examine the architectures on their own modality, Appendix~\ref{app:imu} compares independent implementations on common nominal IMU observations, using causal preprocessing and simple controls. The resulting comparison concerns normal prediction. It neither reproduces the papers' attack benchmarks nor places IMU-only predictors in the same ranking as command-aware recovery monitors.

before: Interval-observer fault detection explicitly considers the effect of uncertain models and observer design~\cite{interval}. Adding a bound to a measured residual, or requiring a dwell period before clearing an alarm, is not by itself a new digital-twin mechanism. The useful question here is whether the resulting decision remains feasible at the tolerance required by the recovery definition.
after: Uncertain models and observer design are already central to interval-observer fault detection~\cite{interval}. Residual bounds and dwell periods are therefore established ingredients. Our concern is their feasibility: after these allowances are applied, can the rule still recognize a return within the chosen tolerance? A rule may be conservative enough to avoid premature clearing yet leave no room to clear at all.

before: The RESCUE preprint evaluates the value of runtime alarms through counterfactual robot-policy interventions~\cite{rescue}. Our evaluator instead compares corrupted and uncorrupted executions of the same plant to measure the disappearance of a motion deviation. The overlap is substantive: counterfactual evaluation is existing methodology. Our narrower emphasis is the interaction among reference error, sensor noise and a particular alarm-clearance rule. The experiments support conclusions about this rule and these simulated conditions, rather than a ranking against complete recent robotic-security systems.
after: The RESCUE preprint uses counterfactual robot-policy interventions to assess whether runtime alarms are worth acting on~\cite{rescue}. It distinguishes detection accuracy from the usefulness of an intervention. We also use a counterfactual, but for a narrower measurement: comparing corrupted and uncorrupted executions of the same plant to determine when a motion deviation ends. Counterfactual evaluation is thus part of the existing methodology on which this study builds. before: The studies distinguish three questions that a single detection score cannot answer: whether unauthorized motion is detected, whether its physical effect persists, and whether the chosen clearance rule can recognize normal motion. The candidate's reduced benign alarm count initially appears favorable, but two plants have an unreachable clearing condition. after: The central failure was easy to miss if judged only by benign alarm counts. The candidate produced fewer such alarms, yet on two plants its clearing condition could never be satisfied. Removing the uncertainty allowance under the same entry threshold gave better outcomes. In this experiment, the added allowance did not earn its place in the rule. The result also separates questions that an interval detection score combines poorly: whether an attack is detected, whether its physical effect remains, and whether the monitor can recognize recovery.

before: Improved commissioning addresses one part of the problem. Longer ARX histories reduce normal prediction error and make Q2's condition reachable. The remaining failure on Q3, together with the perfect-reference calculation, shows that reference bias and measurement noise require separate treatment. A maximum of noisy residuals is not interchangeable with a bound on model error. Once it is added to another noisy residual, the available tolerance can be consumed before any genuine physical deviation is considered.
after: Better commissioning helps, but only to a point. Longer ARX histories lower normal prediction error and make Q2's clearing condition reachable. Q3 still fails. The perfect-reference calculation explains why fitting alone is insufficient: the empirical maximum contains measurement noise as well as model error. Adding that maximum to another noisy residual can use up the tolerance even when there is no physical deviation. Reference bias and measurement noise therefore need separate treatment.

before: This suggests a practical design sequence: define the physical return target and trusted information; check the return condition under normal motion; then evaluate detection, persistence and recovery jointly. Algebraic reachability, point feasibility and successful dwell probes provide different evidence. None alone establishes a safe reset policy. Statistical estimation, averaging and noise-aware observers are established tools for revising such a decision, and a replacement would need comparison against those tools rather than a new name for the present combination.
after: A recovery monitor should first specify what return means and which observations it can trust. The next check is whether its clearing condition is reachable during normal motion. Only then is it useful to examine detection, alarm persistence and recovery together. Algebraic reachability, the fraction of feasible observations and successful dwell probes answer different parts of that question; none alone establishes a safe reset policy. Any replacement should also be tested against ordinary statistical estimation, averaging and noise-aware observers, since these already address parts of the problem.

before: Study III makes this distinction quantitative. A windowed uncertainty control can certify normal residuals that an instantaneous control cannot, while still failing under correlated noise or faster within-tolerance variation. The limiting terms have different meanings: a noise term shrinks with effective sample size, whereas the current-state drift term increases with window length. Ignoring correlation improves some reported certificate fractions by weakening the assumption contract, not by demonstrating more reliable recovery. Useful deployment would require these uncertainty quantities to be justified from commissioning observations and plant knowledge; they were supplied by the generator in Study III.
after: Study III shows what averaging can and cannot repair. Windowed bounds certify some normal residuals that the instantaneous bound cannot certify. With stronger correlation or faster variation within tolerance, that advantage disappears. A longer window reduces the noise term but increases the allowance for change between the window average and the current state. Assuming independent noise when it is correlated makes some certificate fractions look better while removing their statistical justification. Here the generator supplied the uncertainty parameters; an operational monitor would have to justify them from commissioning observations and knowledge of the plant.

A physical deployment would not have that exact counterfactual, so the recovery target would carry uncertainty of its own.

before: Alarm recovery depends on more than prediction accuracy. In the declared simulation, adding an empirical uncertainty allowance halves benign alarm observations relative to nominal fixed return but prevents timely clearance in two-thirds of detected-returned events. The matched control without that allowance performs better. Improved clean-data references reduce discrepancy without restoring feasibility across all plants. The Gaussian analysis identifies how calibration noise consumes the return margin, while the covariance-aware window experiment shows a further trade-off between averaging and current-motion uncertainty. Its criterion is met on 20 of 36 constructed normal traces. The separate IMU comparison also retains a strong ordinary autoregressive control after longer CNN training. Together, these findings support evaluating uncertainty, information access and normal-return feasibility explicitly. They establish neither a universally effective reset policy nor superiority over CASPER.
after: A smaller prediction error does not settle when an attack alarm should clear. In our simulation, the empirical uncertainty allowance halves benign alarm observations relative to nominal fixed return, yet prevents timely clearance in two-thirds of detected-returned events. The matched rule without the allowance performs better. Fitting more accurate references helps, but does not restore feasibility on every plant. Calibration noise can consume the return margin even with a perfect reference, and averaging introduces a further trade-off with uncertainty about current motion. The window control meets its criterion on 20 of 36 constructed normal traces. In the separate IMU study, ordinary autoregression also remains a strong control after longer convolutional neural network (CNN) training. These findings support checking normal-return feasibility and uncertainty assumptions before interpreting a lower alarm count as an improvement. They do not establish a universal reset policy or superiority over CASPER.

after: This file differs from the original CASPER-v3 archive, and its exact correspondence to the original paper's runs remains unresolved. It contains nine channels: X/Y/Z measurements from an accelerometer, gyroscope and magnetometer. We could not resolve the timestamp units or whether they record acquisition or arrival. The filename is therefore insufficient evidence for reporting elapsed time or detection delay.

before: Training uses mean squared error, Adamax at learning rate $10^{-3}$, chronological minibatches without shuffling, and seeds 17,42,2026. All models start afresh for this longer study; optimizer state was not transferred from the short pilot. The maximum is 100 epochs. A development improvement greater than $10^{-6}$ selects a checkpoint; five epochs without such improvement stop training. Per-fit CPU admission is limited to 240 seconds, with total ceilings of 1,200 seconds wall and 900 seconds CPU. No attack labels select training duration, model weights or score formulas.
after: Training uses mean squared error (MSE), Adamax at learning rate $10^{-3}$, chronological minibatches without shuffling, and seeds 17,42,2026. All models start afresh for this longer study; optimizer state was not transferred from the short pilot. The maximum is 100 epochs. A development improvement greater than $10^{-6}$ selects a checkpoint; five epochs without such improvement stop training. Per-fit CPU admission is limited to 240 seconds, with total ceilings of 1,200 seconds wall and 900 seconds CPU. No attack labels select training duration, model weights or score formulas.

before: All CASPER-style seeds stop by the declared patience rule after 27 epochs and select epoch 22, with MSE 0.017451--0.017703. This is 46.11--58.12\% below their respective short-pilot errors. All compact seeds reach 100 epochs while improving, so their MSE 0.042700--0.044730 remains training-limited. AR(4) has the lowest error, 0.006074, on this prefix. Figure~\ref{fig:imu} retains the learning curves for every neural seed.
after: Longer training lowers the CASPER-style errors. Every seed stops under the declared patience rule after 27 epochs and selects epoch 22, with MSE 0.017451--0.017703. These errors are 46.11--58.12\% below the corresponding short-pilot values. The compact models all reach 100 epochs while still improving; their MSE 0.042700--0.044730 remains limited by the training budget. AR(4) gives the lowest error on this prefix, 0.006074. Figure~\ref{fig:imu} includes the learning curve for every neural seed.

before: Median filtering induces dependence and changes the prediction task; the strong autoregressive result therefore cannot be transferred to unfiltered attack detection. Patience stopping is not proof of a global optimum, representative full-data convergence or original-paper reproduction. No attack threshold, F1, recovery score or test-label optimization was computed in this study. Improved normal MSE does not establish a more effective cyberattack detector.
after: These results apply to the filtered normal prefix. Median filtering changes the prediction task and introduces dependence, so the autoregressive advantage cannot be assumed to hold for unfiltered attack detection. The patience rule establishes when these runs stopped, not a global optimum, convergence on a representative full dataset or reproduction of the published experiments. This study computes no attack threshold, F1 or recovery score and performs no test-label optimization. Lower normal MSE alone is insufficient evidence of better cyberattack detection.
